<reflection>
- The previous experiment with high S and high P successfully separated the models, bringing deactivation mechanisms to the top.
- M17 (P + catS -> inactive) and M16 (S + catS -> inactive) are currently the leading models, followed by M11 (S + cat -> inactive), M18 (2catS -> inactive), and M14 (catS -> inactive).
- My aim was achieved: we have narrowed the field to specific deactivation pathways. Now we must distinguish whether the deactivation is driven by substrate (M16, M11), product (M17), or simply the active catalyst state itself (M18, M14).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate between the specific deactivation triggers, I propose an experiment with the maximum substrate concentration ([S] = 5.0), a high catalyst concentration ([cat] = 0.15), and no initial product ([P] = 0.0).
This condition isolates the dependence of the deactivation rate on [S] versus [P] and exploits the saturation of the catalyst.
- For M16 (S + catS -> inactive): The deactivation rate is proportional to [S][catS]. At [S] = 5.0, the catalyst is saturated ([catS] is maxed out), so the deactivation rate scales linearly with the very high [S]. This will cause extremely rapid early deactivation and the reaction will stall at a low final conversion.
- For M17 (P + catS -> inactive): The deactivation rate is proportional to [P][catS]. Since initial [P] = 0, there is zero initial deactivation. The reaction will exhibit a very high initial rate, followed by a pronounced, accelerating slowdown as P accumulates and triggers deactivation.
- For M11 (S + cat -> inactive): The deactivation rate is proportional to [S][cat]. Because the very high [S] drives the catalyst equilibrium almost entirely into the catS state, free [cat] is depleted. This "substrate protection" effect means deactivation will saturate rather than scale linearly with [S], leading to significantly higher conversion than M16.
- For M18 and M14: Deactivation depends only on [catS] or [catS]^2. Since [catS] is saturated at high [S], their deactivation rates will be constant and independent of the linearly increasing [S] or accumulating [P], showing a standard exponential decay of the reaction rate.
</hypothesis>
